items.title: Avakian George — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I got a chance to make an album with Jess Stacy and my great idol of my extreme youth, Earl Hines

ctx.x: That was in the ’50s. That was 1950-who?

That would be very early ’50s, yeah. Wonderful things happened, like I got a chance to make an album with Jess Stacy and my great idol of my extreme youth, Earl Hines, which I never expected to be able to do. That series also led to the signing of Erroll Garner, which came about in an odd way. I just want to back up a little about Erroll and me personally, because I came out of the Army in early 1946. My brother, who was 7 years younger than I, had gone into the Navy after graduating from Yale and going to the…

items.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998
items.q: I only could detect about four musicians that I could recognize, including Earl Hines of course

ctx.x: It wasn’t just in the south either, was it?

No it was I understand pretty much everywhere, but worse in the south of course. That’s a period where I was in school so I didn’t observe that particularly. I never saw Billie on stage with Artie Shaw for example, but I did see Roy Eldridge performing in person with Gene Krupa and there was always a little bit of a stir when Roy came down front to do a vocal duet with Anita O’Day. People would say, “Hey look at that, look, he’s going to sing with her. Well that’s pretty damn naive. Of course we guys who were…
most of the chorus girls. That color business always held forth in the black night clubs in Harlem. They wanted light skinned girls.
